theme: The Good Samaritan; Mary and Martha; teaching on prayer
readingInstruction: Read Luke 9:51-11:13. The journey to Jerusalem begins, and with it the great central section of Luke. Notice the parable of the Good Samaritan, Mary and Martha, and the Lord’s Prayer.
settingTheScene: Luke 9:51 is the hinge of the Gospel: “When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.” From here to chapter 19, most of the material is on the road. Much of it is found only in Luke, including the Good Samaritan, Mary and Martha, and many of the parables. The journey is about discipleship, mercy, and prayer, with the cross ahead.
observation: “When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem” (9:51).
“Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (9:58).
“The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (10:2).
“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself” (10:27).
“But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion” (10:33).
“Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her” (10:42).
“How much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” (11:13).
interpretation:
Jesus sets his face toward Jerusalem. A Samaritan village will not receive him, and James and John want to call down fire. Jesus rebukes them. The way of Jesus is not vengeance. Would-be followers are warned of the cost: no home, no looking back.

Seventy-two others are sent ahead, two by two, with a message of peace and the kingdom. They come back rejoicing, but Jesus says, “Do not rejoice that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” Salvation is a greater joy than power.

A lawyer asks what he must do to inherit eternal life, and Jesus asks what the Law says. The answer is to love God and neighbor. Wanting to justify himself, the lawyer asks, “Who is my neighbor?” Jesus tells of a man beaten by robbers. A priest and a Levite pass by on the other side. A Samaritan, a despised outsider, stops, binds the wounds, pays for the care. Jesus then turns the question around: not “who is my neighbor,” but “who proved to be a neighbor?” The answer is “The one who showed him mercy.” “You go, and do likewise.” Many Christians also see in the story a picture of Christ himself, the outsider who finds us half dead and pays the price. But the point of the story is mercy toward anyone in need.

At Martha and Mary’s house, Martha is busy and anxious, and Mary sits at Jesus’ feet to listen. Jesus does not scold service, but he says Mary has chosen the better thing. Hearing him comes first.

Then a disciple asks, “Lord, teach us to pray.” Jesus gives a short prayer: Father, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, give us bread, forgive us, lead us not into temptation. He tells of the friend at midnight and urges persistence: ask, seek, knock. If earthly fathers give good gifts, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. The best answer to prayer is God himself.
connection: Leviticus 19:18 and Deuteronomy 6:5 are the two commands the lawyer quotes. 2 Kings 1 is Elijah calling down fire, the story James and John echo. Isaiah 50:7 says the Servant set his face like a flint. Matthew 6:9-13 gives the longer version of the Lord’s Prayer. John 4 shows Jesus with a Samaritan woman. Romans 8:15 speaks of the Spirit of adoption by whom we cry, “Abba, Father.” James 2:13 says mercy triumphs over judgment.
application:
Pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly today, one line at a time, adding your own words to each.

Ask who the Samaritan is in your life, a person you are tempted to avoid. Show mercy to them.

Sit at Jesus’ feet for ten quiet minutes before the busyness begins.
prayerPrompts: Pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly in your own words.
Ask him to teach you to sit at his feet as Mary did.
Ask him to show you who your neighbor is.
